title: Case 7
example_chapter:
They buried Great-Aunt Perpetua Lowry on the hottest Thursday of the summer of 1974, in the family plot behind the Methodist church at Sabine Bend, and the whole parish turned out to make sure she was really going in.

I had driven down from Shreveport on four hours of sleep and a borrowed black dress that fit like a bad apology. The church had no air conditioning. It had, instead, forty paper fans printed with the name of Delacroix & Sons Funeral Home, and the sound of them, all those little wings beating in the heat, was the sound of a congregation trying not to say what it thought.

I watched hands. I always do; it is a habit left over from a childhood spent sitting beneath tables. Hands tell you everything the faces are working so hard to hide. Cousin Beau's hands, for instance, kept returning to his breast pocket, where a folded square of paper had made a lump the size of a deck of cards. Aunt Lurleen's hands were clasped around her pocketbook as if it might leap away. And the preacher, Reverend Tolliver, kept patting the lectern with the flat of his right palm, gently, like a man calming a horse he had no intention of riding.

Perpetua herself had been a woman whose hands never rested. She shelled peas by the bushel and mended nets for men who had no use for nets and, in the evenings, laid out solitaire on the porch table in rows so straight you could have hung wash on them. She had raised me, more or less, from the age of nine, and she had never once, in nineteen years, told me what she wanted.

That was the trouble. She had left a will.

It was read in the parlor after the burying, in the heavy, shuttered dark of a house that still smelled of her camphor and her coffee, while the casseroles sweated on the sideboard. Mr. Arceneaux, the lawyer, was a thin man in a seersucker suit who sweated so politely that you wanted to hand him a handkerchief and an apology. He read in a voice meant for the back of a courtroom. The house, to Cousin Beau. The land along the bayou, to Aunt Lurleen. The pecan tree in the side yard, which had stood since before the Civil War and which the entire family believed to be worth less than a good fence post, to me.

"The tree," said Beau.

"The pecan tree," said Mr. Arceneaux, "in the side yard. And, I am instructed to add, everything beneath it."

Nobody said anything for a long moment. The mantel clock, which had been stopped at ten past four since the day my uncle drowned, did not so much as twitch. I understood then what the sound in the church had been. They had come to bury her, yes, but also to be sure that whatever she had been keeping could not go into the ground with her.

"Beneath it," Lurleen repeated, in the tone of a woman reading her own death notice.

"It appears," Mr. Arceneaux said, "to be a figure of speech."

"Perpetua never made a figure of speech in her life," said Beau.

I did not say that she had made one every day, in every ordinary sentence, if you listened for the hands behind them. I did not say that I had seen her, once, at midnight in the winter I was fourteen, kneeling in the leaf-mould under that tree with a trowel and a lantern, burying something no larger than a cigar box and humming a hymn so softly it might have been the wind. I had been standing at the window in my nightgown, and she had turned and looked straight up at the glass, though I was sure I had made no sound, and she had put one finger to her lips.

I had kept that finger, and that silence, for fourteen years. It sat in me now the way the heat sat in that parlor, thick and patient and impossible to breathe around.

"I'll take the tree," I said.

"Of course you will, sugar," said Lurleen, and her hands, those careful hands, let go of her pocketbook at last. "We'd never dream of getting in the way."

It was the kindest thing anyone said all afternoon, and the first time I understood that I was being warned.
